title: Optimization versus fair sampling in quantum annealing: An exactly characterized frustrated Ising benchmark
abstract: Reaching a degenerate ground-state manifold and sampling it uniformly are distinct properties of a quantum annealer. We quantify this distinction using an Ising ring with additional couplings between maximally separated sites. For antiferromagnetic benchmark couplings and $N \geq 5$, we derive the exact ground-state energy, degeneracy, and defect structure for each congruence class of $N$ modulo four. This classification separates ground-state hit probability from conditional sampling bias. We embed instances with up to 162 logical spins on a D-Wave Advantage processor using length-two chains and compare its output with simulated annealing on the embedded and logical problems. For a frustrated $N=83$ instance, the processor visits 164 of the 166 exact ground states, yet the conditional distributions over states and defect sectors remain nonuniform. For $N=160$, the processor has a larger ground-state hit probability than logical simulated annealing (0.869 versus 0.519), but also a larger total-variation distance from uniformity (0.317 versus 0.136). A pause during the anneal raises the ground-state hit probability from 0.42 to 0.86 without restoring uniform sampling. These results identify a relaxation window and demonstrate that optimization success and sampling quality need not improve together, providing an exactly characterized benchmark for open-system quantum annealing.
summary: This paper rigorously benchmarks quantum annealers using a frustrated Ising ring model to separate the concepts of optimization success from fair sampling. By analyzing the ground-state manifold, the authors demonstrate that a high probability of finding the ground state does not imply that the system samples all ground states uniformly. This finding provides a critical diagnostic tool for assessing quantum annealing hardware performance.
main_problem: The paper distinguishes between two distinct properties of quantum annealers: the ability to reach a degenerate ground-state manifold (optimization success) and the ability to sample that manifold uniformly (fair sampling).
main_result: Optimization success does not guarantee fair sampling; the processor can hit the ground state frequently while exhibiting significant, measurable bias in the distribution over those states.
method: The authors use an exactly characterized frustrated Ising model on a ring structure, comparing quantum annealing results against classical simulated annealing on both embedded and logical problems.
model_or_system: The system is an Ising ring with nearest-neighbor and additional couplings between maximally separated sites, described by a specific Hamiltonian. The ground-state manifold structure is analytically determined based on the ring size N modulo four.
key_observables: Ground-state hit probability ($P_G$), total-variation distance ($d_{TV}$) from uniformity, and conditional distributions over defect sectors.
important_parameters: The size of the ring ($N$), the nature of the couplings (antiferromagnetic), and the annealing schedule (including pauses).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the exact analytical knowledge of the ground-state manifold for the specific Ising ring structure.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the ground states and bonds (nearest-neighbor vs. maximally separated) for small N, while other figures compare $P_G$ and sampling bias across different annealing times.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and the two distinct goals (optimization vs. sampling). It then derives the exact ground-state structure analytically based on N mod 4. Finally, it presents numerical results comparing QPU performance to classical methods, demonstrating the decoupling of the two goals.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, exactly characterized benchmark for assessing the limitations of quantum annealers, which is crucial for understanding the practical utility of quantum computation in optimization problems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic picture of representative ground states for the couplings in Eq. (7). Filled and open circles denote spins +1 and −1. Solid and dashed lines represent nearest- neighbor and maximally separated bonds, respectively. Red marks unsatisfied bonds. (a) N = 8: two antipodal nearest- neighbor defects, with all maximally separated bonds satis- fied. (b),(d) N = 9, 7: one nearest-neighbor defect, with five and three unsatisfied maximally separated bonds, respec- tively. (c) N = 10: a N´eel state satisfying all bonds.

FIG. 2. Ground-state hit probability PG of the QPU as a function of the annealing time for representative system sizes in the four congruence classes of N modulo four: (a) N ≡0, (b) N ≡1, (c) N ≡2, and (d) N ≡3 (mod 4). The vertical dashed line at 0.1 µs marks the upper end of the fast-anneal range used here; the longer-time points correspond to standard annealing. The larger instances exhibit a pronounced increase in PG with increasing standard annealing time.

FIG. 3. State-level total-variation distance dst TV from the uniform distribution over exact ground states for represen- tative instances. “SA” denotes simulated annealing on the embedded physical problem, “logical SA” denotes simulated annealing directly on the logical problem, and the QPU re- sults use a standard 20 µs anneal. A smaller value indicates a distribution closer to uniformity. The comparison shows that a protocol with a larger ground-state hit probability need not sample the degenerate ground-state manifold more uniformly.

FIG. 4. Pause-annealing results for N = 83 with a 100 µs pause. (a) Ground-state hit probability PG, (b) state-level total- variation distance dst TV, and (c) sector-level total-variation distance dsec TV as functions of the pause location sp. The horizontal dashed lines denote the corresponding values for the standard 20 µs baseline acquired with the pause data. (d) Conditional probabilities of the 83 defect sectors for the standard anneal and the refined pause locations; each row is normalized over the exact ground-state samples in that data set. The pause produces a pronounced enhancement of PG near sp ≃0.4, while the conditional state and defect-sector distributions remain nonuniform.
